<reason>A wins by distinguishing lower production costs from lower consumer prices, while explicitly accounting for genuine merger-specific efficiencies. It also answers uncertainty about innovation screening without claiming perfect foresight. B offers legitimate scale and commercialization benefits, but repeatedly treats them as certain and miscasts A’s conditional concession as surrender. Its remaining-scaled-rivals defense does not establish that those rivals replace the competitive constraint eliminated by a merger. A therefore supplies the stronger comparative case, though the aggregate magnitude remains uncertain.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s strongest rebuttal was that consumers need not lose every alternative for eliminating a close substitute to raise prices. B’s appeal to existing scaled rivals partly answered the entry-barrier challenge, but not this substitution and pass-through problem. Its cost-floor argument established what a merged firm could charge, not what it would profitably charge.</best_rebuttal>
